en: The Apadāna of the Elder Rattipupphiya Kumuda Chapter, Number 3 [The Elder Rattipupphiya’s Apadāna] In the past, during the time of the Buddha Kassapa, I was a monk dwelling in the forest. One night, while walking for alms, I saw a woman who had gathered flowers. She was adorned with various garlands, And she wore a beautiful robe. Seeing her, I spoke these words: “O lady, from where have you come? “I have come from the city,” she replied, “Carrying these flowers for the sake of worship. Hearing her words, I felt great joy, And I took those flowers from her hand. Then, having taken them, I offered them To the Teacher, the Great Sage. Having made that offering, I passed away And was reborn in the realm of the Thirty-three gods. There I enjoyed divine pleasures For eighty-four thousand years. When my lifespan there had ended, I was reborn in the human world. In this world, I was born into a noble family, Possessing great wealth and prosperity. I was handsome, endowed with beauty, And possessed of all the marks of excellence. I was skilled in the arts and crafts, And I was well-versed in the Vedas. I was beloved by the people, And I was honored by the king. At that time, the Teacher, the Great Sage, Was wandering through the land of Magadha. Hearing that he had arrived in our village, I went out to meet him with great joy. Having approached the Teacher, the Great Sage, I paid homage at his feet. Then, having circumambulated him three times, I sat down to one side. Seated there, I heard the Dhamma, Which was sweet and full of meaning. Having heard the Dhamma, I felt great faith, And I took refuge in the Triple Gem. I gave up the life of a householder And became a renunciant. Having gone forth, I practiced the holy life With diligence and great effort. I observed the precepts perfectly, And I was devoted to meditation. Through the power of that wholesome deed, I attained the fruit of Arhatship. Today, I am an Arhat, free from defilements, With a mind liberated like a lamp extinguished. This is the result of that offering of flowers, Made long ago to the Great Sage. Thus did the Elder Rattipupphiya Speak of his own former deeds. Having heard this account of his past lives, The assembly of monks rejoiced greatly.
“In the past, I was a deer-hunter in the forest wilderness;
there I saw Vipassī, the Buddha.”
Having seen the *kuṭaja* tree, a blossom of the earth, red and in full bloom, [he praised] the God of Gods, the Bull among Men.
Having grasped it by its very root,
I offered it to the Great Sage.
I do not know a state of misery;
this is the fruit of the gift of flowers.
And in this eighth aeon, one named Suppasanna,
endowed with the seven treasures, [will become a wheel-turning monarch].
I was a king of great power.
[I attained] the four analytical knowledges... [and so forth].
“Thus was the teaching of the Buddha spoken.
In this way, it is said, the venerable elder Rattipupphiya recited these verses.
This is the third legend (Apadāna) of the elder Rattipupphiya.
